Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The export covers six blocks around Cedar Square and includes responses collected from March 4 through April 29. It has 186 completed forms and 12 partial forms, and the partial forms remain in a separate tab. The file name is cedar_square_survey_april_final, and the tab names are Overview, Responses, Access Notes, and Follow Up. The word “final” is part of the file name, but the group has not marked the export as approved. This is the version prepared by Mara Ellis after she checked the response count against the paper intake log.

At the top of Overview, the survey asks residents how they use the square during an ordinary week. The choices are walking through, attending events, sitting outdoors, and using the play area. People could select more than one choice, and there was also a write-in box. The largest number of selections was for walking through, followed by sitting outdoors. The export does not calculate a single total of residents for those answers because one form can include several selections. Mara said the percentages are based on completed forms and should not be read as a count of unique visitors. That note is already in the first row of the Overview tab.

The Responses tab has the original answer text beside a short category assigned for sorting. The category is not meant to replace what the resident wrote. For example, one response says, “The path is easy in the morning, but the benches fill up after school,” and its category is “seating and timing.” Another resident wrote, “I can hear the music from my apartment, but I cannot get across the square with my walker,” and the category is “route access.” Mara kept both comments in the export because the first mentions a time of day and the second describes a barrier that may not appear in a checkbox answer. No names or apartment numbers are included in that tab.

The Access Notes tab has four records that need a closer look before anyone uses the figures in a public handout. Two residents left the question about mobility blank, one response lists both the west gate and the fountain as an entry point, and one paper form has a date written as April 31. The date is outside the calendar, but the paper log shows that it arrived with the April 30 batch. Mara has not changed that record. She added a note saying “date needs checking,” so the original entry remains visible while the records group decides how to describe it in the export.

The survey invitation was available in English, Spanish, and Somali at the library desk and at the Saturday market. Volunteers entered the paper forms during two evening sessions and checked each other by reading the totals aloud. The market table was moved indoors once because of heavy rain, but the forms collected that day stayed in the same batch number. The survey did not ask for a home address or a phone number, and the optional comment box contains two references to nearby storefronts that are already named in the public directory. One volunteer asked whether those references should be removed. Mara left them as written and flagged them for a later review.

Delivery notes
1. The export was saved as a spreadsheet and as a comma-separated file. The comma-separated copy opens with the response text in one wide column on some older office computers. The spreadsheet has wrapped text turned on for the comment column.
2. The date field uses year-month-day order, and the export timestamp is May 2 at 9:12 in the morning.
3. The paper intake log is in a blue folder at the library service desk and is not included with the files.
4. If the group sends a public handout before the date question is checked, then leave out the count for that record and keep the note about the April batch attached to the internal copy. The count can be revisited after the paper form is found.

The shared folder has a read-only copy for the library team and an editable working copy for the records group. Mara said, “Please keep the working copy in the survey folder and add comments there rather than changing the read-only file.” She also said that if the library asks for a second export before the open house, then use the same six-block boundary and include the partial forms tab only if the request specifically asks for partial responses. The current handout draft uses the completed form total and has no map attached. There is not yet a confirmed date for printing.

One concern raised at the evening check was that residents might treat the category labels as official findings. The records group has not decided whether those labels will appear outside the internal spreadsheet. The labels came from a short sorting guide written for this survey and were not tested as a standard classification. The guide says route access includes comments about crossings, curb ramps, and paths, and seating and timing includes remarks about benches, shade, and busy periods. If anyone quotes a response in a handout, the group will need to check that the wording can be understood without the question printed beside it.

The open house table is planned for the east room at the library, and the survey team has reserved space for a one-page summary and a sheet explaining how people can submit corrections. The room has two doors, and the entrance nearest the lift is the one volunteers intend to use. If the lift is unavailable, the east room can still be reached by the short ramp from the courtyard, but the event coordinator has not confirmed whether that ramp will be open after six in the evening. The event sign should give both the room name and the library address because the market volunteers said several residents came to the wrong building last time.

The forwarding note should say that this is a working export for review and that the figures describe the responses received during the stated collection dates. The note should not describe the survey as a vote or imply that the comments represent every resident. Mara asked the records group to reply with questions about the Access Notes tab before the open house packet is assembled. If there are no questions, the spreadsheet can remain in the shared folder without another version being made. The paper intake log and the flagged storefront references still need their separate review, and the final file name alone does not settle either issue."}]
